figures.caption: Figure 1: Cross-dataset visual-fMRI harmonization and the BRAID-fMRI model. a, Visual stimuli are presented during fMRI acquisition, and single-trial responses are estimated to obtain stimulus-specific brain activity patterns. b, Eight visual-fMRI datasets spanning static-image and dynamic-video experiments are brought into a common processing framework. fMRI responses are represented using 360 HCP-MMP1.0 cortical parcels and 19 additional regions, while stimuli are represented in a common 512-dimensional CLIP ViT-B/32 image space. c, ROI-wise responses from participants in eight visual-fMRI datasets are mapped to ROI tokens and augmented with learned ROI embeddings and, in participant-conditioned analyses, learned participant embeddings. A Transformer shared across datasets and participants contextualizes the tokens, which are attention-pooled and projected into the 512-dimensional image space of a frozen CLIP ViT-B/32 encoder. Participant embeddings are omitted in the zero-shot transfer experiments. A multi-positive contrastive objective aligns neural responses with their corresponding stimuli while treating repeated observations of the same stimulus as positives.

Figure 2: Cross-dataset and within-dataset stimulus retrieval. a, Dataset-level unique-stimulus Top-10 retrieval using a global candidate pool comprising all unique validation stimuli across the seven evaluation datasets. Filled circles show observed accuracy with query-level 95% Wilson confidence intervals, which do not account for within-participant or within-session dependence; open diamonds denote global chance. Adjacent summaries show performance relative to chance (× chance), median rank of the correct stimulus (lower is better), and the numbers of candidate stimuli and retrieval queries. b, Participant-level Top-10 retrieval using the same global candidate pool. Participants are ordered by accuracy within each dataset; filled circles and error bars show observed accuracy and 95% Wilson confidence intervals, and dashed lines indicate dataset means. NOD is omitted for visual clarity because of its larger participant sample. c, Participant-level retrieval with the candidate pool restricted to unique validation stimuli from the query participant’s dataset. Filled circles and error bars show observed accuracy and 95% Wilson confidence intervals; open circles denote participant-specific chance levels and vertical connectors show the difference from chance. Dashed lines indicate dataset means. NOD is shown separately in a wider lower panel. d, Each row shows the true stimulus followed by the ten highest-ranked candidates based on cosine similarity between the predicted brain embedding and frozen CLIP ViT-B/32 image embeddings. Green borders and check marks identify the true stimulus. Examples span multiple datasets; high-ranking non-matches often share object category, scene context, shape or texture with the target, illustrating the semantic structure of the learned retrieval space. HAD dataset is not presented since it is not included in the retrieval evaluation.
Table 1: Participant-matched unique-stimulus Top-10 retrieval accuracy.

Figure 3: Semantic organization, network contributions and zero-shot cross-dataset transfer. a, t-SNE visualization of 40 k-means clusters obtained from normalized CLIP embeddings of unique validation stimuli. Ten clusters used for subsequent analyses are highlighted, with representative stimuli shown. b, Dataset composition of the selected clusters. Stacked bars show the number of unique stimuli contributed by each dataset. Cluster labels (C0–C39) denote arbitrary k-means cluster identifiers and are unrelated to retrieval rank; ranks indicate ordering by Top-10 retrieval accuracy. c, Top: unique-stimulus Top-10 accuracy for all clusters, ordered by performance; bottom: number of unique stimuli in the same ordering. Every fourth cluster in the ranked sequence was retained, yielding ten clusters spanning the full performance range. d, Global unique-stimulus Top-10 accuracy after masking each functional or anatomical ROI group. The dashed line marks the unablated baseline; annotations give percentage-point changes. e, Dataset-specific ablation effects. f, Participant-level effects for the four most disruptive groups. Points denote participants, violins show distributions, boxes show medians and interquartile ranges, and black circles show means. Asterisks denote one-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank tests of retrieval impairment, with Benjamini–Hochberg correction across nine groups. g, Zero-shot participant and dataset transfer with participant embeddings disabled throughout training and evaluation. For each target, the entire dataset and all of its participants remain held out while source datasets and participants are cumulatively added to pretraining. Values are percentage changes relative to step 0; annotations report the net change from the first to the final step.

Figure 4: CLIP-space semantic organization and category-associated attribution patterns. a, Brain–CLIP cosine similarity for the matched stimulus, a non-matching stimulus from the same semantic cluster and a stimulus from a different cluster. Thin lines show participant-level or dataset-level trajectories, and summary markers show the group mean with uncertainty. b, Participant-level identity and semantic margins for the ten representative clusters, defined as matched minus same-cluster similarity and same-cluster minus different-cluster similarity, respectively. c, The same margins summarized by dataset. d, Cluster-associated ROI beta patterns projected onto the HCP-MMP1.0 cortical surface for ten representative semantic clusters. Colours indicate normalized cluster-associated beta values. e, Network composition of positively cluster-selective saliency. Radar plots show observed counts among up to 20 positively selective ROIs in each network for individual clusters; the central bar plot shows observed minus expected counts after correcting for network size. Positive values indicate enrichment. f, Cluster-specific change in unique-stimulus Top-10 accuracy after ablating each functional or anatomical network. Values are ablated minus baseline accuracy in percentage points; negative values indicate that the ablated network supported retrieval.

Figure 5: Semantic organization and robustness of the learned brain representation. a, Hierarchical structure within the learned brain-embedding space. Brain–brain cosine similarity is compared across participant pairs for the same stimulus, different stimuli from the same CLIP-derived semantic cluster, and stimuli from different clusters. Points distinguish participant pairs drawn from the same or different datasets; summary markers show the mean and 95% bootstrap confidence interval. b, Cross-dataset correspondence of semantic representational geometry. Within each dataset, a representational dissimilarity matrix (RDM) was constructed from cosine distances among semantic-cluster centroids. Cells report Spearman correlations between RDMs for dataset pairs with at least five shared semantic clusters. Asterisks denote significance after Benjamini–Hochberg correction of Mantel-style permutation tests; dashes indicate insufficient cluster overlap. c, Expected retrieval performance as the candidate search space increases. For each query, exact expected Top-10 accuracy was derived from its full-pool rank using the hypergeometric distribution. Coloured curves show dataset means, the black curve shows the mean across participants, and shading denotes the 95% bootstrap confidence interval. The dashed line indicates random Top-10 chance, min(10/N, 1), for a candidate pool of size N . d, Retrieval among semantic hard negatives. The fraction of distractors drawn from the same semantic cluster as the target was increased from 0 to 100% while candidate-pool size remained fixed. Expected Top-10 accuracy was computed analytically from the numbers of same- and different-cluster candidates outranking each target. Coloured curves show dataset means, the black curve shows the mean across participants, shading denotes the 95% bootstrap confidence interval and the dashed line indicates random Top-10 chance. e, Preservation of local semantic neighbourhoods. Predicted brain embeddings were averaged across repeated observations of each unique stimulus. For each neighbourhood size k, overlap between the k nearest neighbours in brain and CLIP space was computed across unique stimuli. The black curve shows mean observed overlap with its 95% bootstrap confidence interval; the dashed curve shows the analytical expectation under random neighbourhood correspondence.
